Maximum Edge Open Packing on AT-Free, Chordal, and Convex Bipartite Graphs

**Abstract**

An edge open packing is a set of edges whose endpoints induce a disjoint union of stars. We study the problem of finding a maximum edge open packing in AT-free, chordal, and convex bipartite graphs. For AT-free graphs, we use the oriented star-conflict graph _A<sub>G</sub>_, introduced by Das and Santra, for which \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^o(G)=\alpha(A_G)\), and prove that _A<sub>G</sub>_ is AT-free whenever _G_ is AT-free. Consequently, a known maximum independent set algorithm for AT-free graphs yields an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm for Maximum Edge Open Packing, where _n_ and _m_ denote the numbers of vertices and edges of _G_, respectively. For chordal graphs, we develop an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time dynamic programming algorithm over a nice tree decomposition derived from a clique tree, exploiting the structural fact that the endpoint set of an edge open packing intersects every clique in at most two vertices. Finally, for convex bipartite graphs, we obtain an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time dynamic programming algorithm based on two boundary indices that separate consecutive star components. This result extends the previously known algorithm for biconvex bipartite graphs and, in particular, provides an improved explicit running-time bound for that class.

**Keywords:** Edge open packing; Induced matching; AT-free graphs; Chordal graphs; Convex bipartite graphs; Maximum independent set; Dynamic programming

## 1 Introduction

An induced matching selects edges whose endpoints induce a matching. It is a standard model for choosing mutually isolated interactions and has been studied extensively in graph algorithms [7, 17, 11]. Edge open packing, introduced by Chelladurai et al. [9], allows several selected edges to share a common centre while retaining separation between different components. For example, all _t_ edges of a star _K_<sub>1_,t_</sub> form an edge open packing, whereas an induced matching contains at most one of them.

One motivation comes from channel assignment under a secondary-interference model in packet radio networks [9, 8]. In this model, two selected links conflict when a third link joins their endpoints. A maximum edge open packing is therefore a largest feasible set of links for one channel, and the colour classes of an injective edge colouring are edge open packings. The model permits several links with a shared star centre. More abstractly, it describes the selection of mutually isolated groups of interactions, each organised around one hub.

Formally, let _G_=(_V,E_) be a graph. Two distinct edges have a _common edge_ if an edge other than those two joins an endpoint of one to an endpoint of the other. An _edge open packing_ is a set \(D\subseteq E\) in which no two distinct edges have a common edge. Its maximum cardinality is the _edge open packing number_, denoted by \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^o(G)\), and the optimisation problem of finding such a set is called Maximum Edge Open Packing. If _V(D_) denotes the endpoints of the edges in _D_, then _D_ is an edge open packing precisely when the connected components of _G[V(D_)] are stars, including single edges. Thus, the problem extends induced matching by permitting larger star components.

Brešar and Samadi [5] proved that the decision version is NP-complete on restricted classes including planar graphs of maximum degree four and Eulerian bipartite graphs, and gave a linear-time algorithm for trees. Structural work relates edge open packing to induced matching, diameter, minimum degree,

<tbc>and clique number \[4, 9, 18\]. Santra \[19\] obtained polynomial-time algorithms for proper interval, block, and split graphs. Bhyravarapu et al. \[1\] gave polynomial-time algorithms for distance-hereditary and biconvex bipartite graphs, with an explicit _O(n_<sup>42</sup>) bound for the latter class. They also obtained a \(2^{O(\omega)}\mathrm{poly}(n)\)-time algorithm on chordal graphs, where \(\omega\) is the clique number.

Das and Santra \[13\] introduced the _oriented star-conflict graph A<sub>G</sub>_ and established the identity \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{o}(G)=\alpha(A_G)\). The vertices of _A<sub>G</sub>_ correspond to oriented edges of _G_, where the first endpoint is designated as the centre of a star and the second as one of its leaves; the precise adjacency rule is recalled in Section 3. Using this construction, they obtained _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithms for permutation and interval graphs, where _n_=|_V(G_)| and _m_=|_E(G_)|; in terms of _n_ alone, this gives an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>) bound \[13\]. They treated well-partitioned chordal graphs separately.

More recently, Das and Santra \[12\] used the same oriented star-conflict graph to study Maximum Edge Open Packing on cocomparability graphs. They proved that if _G_ is a cocomparability graph, then _A<sub>G</sub>_ is also a cocomparability graph. Since maximum independent set is polynomial-time solvable on cocomparability graphs, this yields an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>2</sup>)-time algorithm, and hence an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm in terms of _n_ alone \[12\]. This result simultaneously generalizes the earlier algorithms for permutation and interval graphs, since both classes are contained in the class of cocomparability graphs.

The present work takes this structural approach one step further. We prove that the transformation \(G\mapsto A_G\) preserves AT-freeness: if _G_ is AT-free, then so is _A<sub>G</sub>_. Since cocomparability graphs form a subclass of AT-free graphs, this extends the oriented star-conflict framework to a strictly broader setting. The graph _A<sub>G</sub>_ has 2_m_ vertices and can be constructed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>2</sup>) time. Applying the _O(N_<sup>4</sup>)-time maximum independent set algorithm of Broersma et al. \[6\] to _A<sub>G</sub>_, where _N_=|_V(A<sub>G</sub>_)|=2_m_, gives an overall running time of _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>), which is _O(n_<sup>8</sup>) when expressed only in terms of _n_. The progression of these results and the corresponding graph-class inclusions are illustrated in Figure 1.

## Our contributions.

We give polynomial-time algorithms for three graph classes. First, we prove that _A<sub>G</sub>_ is AT-free whenever _G_ is AT-free. Combining this preservation theorem with the correspondence of Das and Santra and the independent-set algorithm of Broersma et al. \[6\] yields an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm for Maximum Edge Open Packing, where _n_=|_V(G_)| and _m_=|_E(G_)|.

Second, we give an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm for chordal graphs, without a bound on the clique number. We use a standard nice tree decomposition obtained from a clique tree \[16\]. The endpoint set of an edge open packing meets each clique in at most two vertices. Recording these vertices and their roles in a partially constructed star gives quadratically many states per bag and a constant number of label combinations for each active subset at a join.

Third, we give an _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm for convex bipartite graphs. Convexity orders the connected components of a solution from left to right. Two boundary indices record all restrictions on the next component, allowing a dynamic program that appends one star at a time. This extends the earlier biconvex result to a larger class and improves its explicit running-time bound. These extensions are<tbc>

## 2 Preliminaries

All graphs are finite, simple, and undirected. For a graph _G_, write _n_=|_V(G_)| and _m_=|_E(G_)|. The open and closed neighbourhoods of a vertex _v_ are _N<sub>G</sub>(v_) and _N<sub>G</sub>_\[_v_\], respectively. For \(U\subseteq V(G)\), _G_\[_U_\] denotes the subgraph induced by _U_. An independent set consists of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and \(\alpha(G)\) is its maximum size. For \(D\subseteq E(G)\), let _V(D_) be the set of endpoints of its edges. Throughout the paper, a _star_ means _K_<sub>1_,t_</sub> with \(t\ge 1\). In particular, _K_<sub>2</sub> is a star, and either endpoint may be chosen as its centre. A star with at least two edges has a unique centre.

We use the edge open packing definition from the introduction. The following characterisation also specifies exactly which edges are selected.

**Observation 1.** _An edge set_ \(D\subseteq E(G)\) _is an edge open packing if and only if every connected component of G_\[_V(D_)\] _is a star. In this case, E(G_\[_V(D_)\])=_D._

_Proof._ If _D_ is an edge open packing, an edge in _E(G_\[_V(D_)\])\\_D_ would join two distinct selected edges incident with its endpoints. Hence _E(G_\[_V(D_)\])=_D_. This graph contains neither a triangle nor a path with three edges as a subgraph: in either case one edge is common to two others. A connected graph with an edge and neither of these subgraphs is a star. Conversely, if every component of _G_\[_V(D_)\] is a star, each leaf belongs to _V(D_), so its unique incident edge must belong to _D_. Thus all star edges are selected, and no third edge joins two of them in the forbidden way.

A graph is _chordal_ if it has no induced cycle of length at least four. Its maximal cliques admit a _clique tree_: for each vertex _v_, the maximal cliques containing _v_ induce a connected subtree \[14, 15\]. An _asteroidal triple_ is an independent set {_u,v,w_} such that each pair is joined by a path avoiding the closed neighbourhood of the third vertex. A graph is _AT-free_ if it contains no asteroidal triple.

A bipartite graph \(G=(X\cup Y,E)\) is _convex bipartite_ if one part, say _X_, admits an ordering _x_<sub>1</sub>_,...,x<sub>p</sub>_ in which every neighbourhood _N(y_), \(y\in Y\) , is consecutive. After deleting isolated vertices, write \(N(y)=\{x_{\ell(y)},\dots,x_{r(y)}\}\) with \(1\le\ell(y)\le r(y)\le p\). A convex ordering can be found by testing the consecutive- ones property of the bipartite adjacency matrix \[2\]. A graph is _biconvex bipartite_ if both parts admit such orderings. A _bipartite permutation graph_ is a bipartite graph whose vertices can be represented by line segments between two parallel lines, with adjacency corresponding to intersection. A bipartite graph is _chordal bipartite_ if it has no induced cycle of length at least six.

The standard strict inclusion chain is bipartite permutation graphs \(\unknown\) biconvex bipartite graphs \(\unknown\) convex bipartite graphs \(\unknown\) chordal bipartite graphs \[3\]. Bipartite permutation graphs are AT-free, but biconvex graphs need not be. For example, take a cycle _abcda_ and add pendant vertices \(a',b',c',d'\) at the corresponding cycle vertices. The two part orders \((b',a,c,d')\) and \((a',b,d,c')\) show that this graph is biconvex, whereas \(\{a',b',c'\}\) is an asteroidal triple. Consequently, our AT-free result does not subsume the earlier biconvex result. A claw with each edge subdivided once is convex but not biconvex: order its three subdivision vertices on one side to obtain convexity; on the other side, making each pair consisting of the original centre and an original leaf consecutive would require the centre to be consecutive with three different vertices.

## 3 Maximum Edge Open Packing in AT-Free Graphs

We use the oriented star-conflict graph of Das and Santra \[13\] to reduce Maximum Edge Open Packing on an AT-free graph to Maximum Independent Set on another AT-free graph.

### 3.1 The oriented star-conflict graph

We recall the construction from \[13\]. An _oriented edge_ of _G_ is an ordered pair \((c,\ell)\) such that \(c\ell\in E(G)\). The _oriented star-conflict graph A<sub>G</sub>_ has all oriented edges of _G_ as its vertices. Two distinct oriented edges \((c,\ell)\) and (_d,r_) are _compatible_ if one of the following conditions holds.

(i) They have the same centre: _c=d_, \(\ell\neq r\), and \(\ell r\notin E(G)\).<tbc>

(ii) The vertices \(c,\ell,d,r\) are all distinct, and none of the four pairs \(cd,cr,\ell d,\ell r\) is an edge of _G_.<tbc>

Two vertices of _A<sub>G</sub>_ are adjacent if and only if they are incompatible. In particular, \((c,\ell)\) and \((\ell,c)\) are adjacent, so an independent set cannot select both orientations of one edge. The first coordinate specifies the centre of a selected star and the second specifies a leaf; for a single-edge component, either endpoint may serve as its centre.

**Lemma 2** (\[13\])**.** _For every graph G,_ \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{o}(G)=\alpha(A_G)\).

_Proof._ For completeness, let _D_ be an edge open packing. By Observation 1, the connected components of _G_\[_V(D_)\] are stars. Orient their edges from centre to leaf, choosing either centre for each _K_<sub>2</sub>. The resulting |_D_| oriented edges satisfy the two compatibility rules and form an independent set in _A<sub>G</sub>_. Conversely, an independent set _I_ contains at most one orientation of each edge. Its members with a common first coordinate describe a star with pairwise nonadjacent leaves. Those with different first coordinates have disjoint endpoint sets with no edge between them. Thus their |_I_| underlying edges form an edge open packing, proving the equality.

For example, let _G=C_<sub>5</sub> with vertices _v_<sub>0</sub>_,...,v_<sub>4</sub> in cyclic order, and read subscripts modulo five. Write _a<sub>i</sub>_=(_v<sub>i</sub>,v_<sub>_i_-1</sub>) and _b<sub>i</sub>_=(_v<sub>i</sub>,v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>). The pair _a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_ is compatible for each _i_. Oriented edges with different centres are incompatible, since _C_<sub>5</sub> has no induced 2_K_<sub>2</sub>. Hence <o>_A<sub>G</sub>_</o>=5_K_<sub>2</sub>, or equivalently _A<sub>G</sub>=K_<sub>2,2,2,2,2</sub>, with parts {_a<sub>i</sub>,b<sub>i</sub>_}. In particular, \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{o}(C_5)=\alpha(A_{C_5})=2\). Figure 2 shows the complement to display the compatibility pairs without drawing all forty conflict edges.

## 3.2 Preservation of AT-freeness

**Theorem 3.** _If G is AT-free, then A<sub>G</sub> is AT-free._

_Proof._ We prove the contrapositive. Suppose that _A<sub>G</sub>_ contains an asteroidal triple {_e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub>}, where \(e_i=(c_i,\ell_i)\) for \(i\in\{1,2,3\}\). Since the three vertices are pairwise nonadjacent in _A<sub>G</sub>_, the corresponding oriented edges are pairwise compatible. Therefore, \(\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\) are distinct and pairwise nonadjacent in _G_.

We show that \(\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\}\) is an asteroidal triple in _G_. Fix distinct \(i,j,k\in\{1,2,3\}\). Since {_e_<sub>1</sub>_,e_<sub>2</sub>_,e_<sub>3</sub>} is an asteroidal triple in _A<sub>G</sub>_, there is an _e<sub>i</sub>-e<sub>j</sub>_ path in _A<sub>G</sub>_ avoiding _N<sub>A<sub>G</sub></sub>_\[_e<sub>k</sub>_\]. Write this path as _P=e<sub>i</sub>=f_<sub>0</sub>_,f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>t</sub>=e<sub>j</sub>_, where _f<sub>s</sub>_=(_a<sub>s</sub>,b<sub>s</sub>_), and write \(e_k=(c_k,\ell_k)\). For \(0\le s\le t\), put _R<sub>s</sub>_={_b<sub>s</sub>_} if _a<sub>s</sub>=c<sub>k</sub>_, and _R<sub>s</sub>_={_a<sub>s</sub>,b<sub>s</sub>_} otherwise.

Every vertex _f<sub>s</sub>_ of _P_ is compatible with _e<sub>k</sub>_. If _a<sub>s</sub>=c<sub>k</sub>_, then compatibility of (_c<sub>k</sub>,b<sub>s</sub>_) and \((c_k,\ell_k)\) gives \(b_s\neq\ell_k\) and \(b_s\ell_k\notin E(G)\). If \(a_s\neq c_k\), compatibility gives \(a_s,b_s\notin N_G[\ell_k]\). Hence, \(R_s\cap N_G[\ell_k]=\varnothing\) for every _s_.

We next claim that consecutive sets _R<sub>s</sub>_ and _R_<sub>_s_+1</sub> touch in _G_; that is, they intersect or an edge of _G_ has one endpoint in each set. Suppose otherwise. Write _f<sub>s</sub>_=(_a,b_) and _f_<sub>_s_+1</sub>=(_d,r_). If _a=d=c<sub>k</sub>_, then _R<sub>s</sub>_={_b_} and _R_<sub>_s_+1</sub>={_r_}; the assumption gives \(b\neq r\) and \(br\notin E(G)\), so the two oriented edges are compatible by the same-centre rule. If \(a=d\neq c_k\), then both sets contain _a_, contrary to their being disjoint.

Now suppose that \(a\neq d\). If neither _a_ nor _d_ equals _c<sub>k</sub>_, then _R<sub>s</sub>_={_a,b_} and _R_<sub>_s_+1</sub>={_d,r_}. Their disjointness and the absence of an edge between them show that _a,b,d,r_ are distinct and that all four cross edges are absent. Thus, _f<sub>s</sub>_ and _f_<sub>_s_+1</sub> are compatible. If _a=c<sub>k</sub>_, then _R<sub>s</sub>_={_b_} and _R_<sub>_s_+1</sub>={_d,r_}. The assumption gives \(b\neq d,r\) and \(bd,br\notin E(G)\). Compatibility of (_d,r_) with \((c_k,\ell_k)\) gives \(c_k\neq d,r\) and \(c_kd,c_kr\notin E(G)\). Again the two oriented edges are compatible. The case _d=c<sub>k</sub>_ is symmetric.

In every case, _f<sub>s</sub>_ and _f_<sub>_s_+1</sub> would be compatible, contradicting their adjacency on _P_. Hence consecutive sets touch. Each _R<sub>s</sub>_ induces a connected subgraph, and therefore \(G[\bigcup_{s=0}^tR_s]\) is connected. It contains \(\ell_i\) and \(\ell_j\) and avoids \(N_G[\ell_k]\). Thus, there is an \(\ell_i\)-\(\ell_j\) path avoiding \(N_G[\ell_k]\).

The indices _i,j,k_ were arbitrary. Therefore, \(\{\ell_1,\ell_2,\ell_3\}\) is an asteroidal triple in _G_. Hence, if _A<sub>G</sub>_ contains an asteroidal triple, then so does _G_, proving the contrapositive.

### 3.3 Algorithm and running time

Given an AT-free graph _G_, construct _A<sub>G</sub>_. By Theorem 3, _A<sub>G</sub>_ is AT-free, and by Lemma 2, \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{o}(G)=\alpha(A_G)\). We compute a maximum independent set of _A<sub>G</sub>_ using the algorithm of Broersma et al. \[6\] and translate it back into an edge open packing of _G_ as in the proof of Lemma 2.

**Theorem 4.** _The_ Maximum Edge Open Packing _problem can be solved in O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>) _time on an AT-free graph with n vertices and m edges. In particular, the running time is O(n_<sup>8</sup>) _when expressed only in terms of n._

_Proof._ The graph _A<sub>G</sub>_ has one vertex for each oriented edge of _G_, so |_V(A<sub>G</sub>_)|=2_m_. An adjacency matrix of _G_ can be constructed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) time, after which compatibility of two oriented edges can be tested in constant time. Thus, _A<sub>G</sub>_ can be constructed in _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>2</sup>) time.

The algorithm of Broersma et al. \[6\] solves Maximum Independent Set on an _N_-vertex AT-free graph in _O(N_<sup>4</sup>) time. Applying it with _N_=2_m_ takes _O(m_<sup>4</sup>) time. Translating the independent set back into an edge open packing takes _O(m_) time. The total running time is therefore _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>), which is _O(n_<sup>8</sup>) because _m=O(n_<sup>2</sup>).

## 4 Maximum Edge Open Packing in Chordal Graphs

In this section, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for chordal graphs. Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a chordal graph on _n_ vertices. If _G_ is disconnected, we solve the problem independently on its connected components and add the optimum values. We therefore assume throughout the description that _G_ is connected.

Let T be a clique tree of _G_. From T , we construct a nice rooted tree decomposition (_T,_B) whose root and leaves have empty bags and whose nodes are leaf, introduce, forget, or join nodes. Along an edge between two maximal cliques, vertices are first forgotten down to the intersection and then introduced up to the other clique. Join nodes use copies of one maximal clique. Thus, every bag of the nice decomposition is a subset of a maximal clique and is therefore a clique. The standard transformation has _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) nodes \[16\].

For \(t\in V(T)\), let _B<sub>t</sub>_ be its bag, let _T<sub>t</sub>_ be the subtree rooted at _t_, and let _G<sub>t</sub>_ be the subgraph of _G_ induced by all vertices occurring in bags of _T<sub>t</sub>_. We use the following separation properties. If _t_ is an introduce node with child \(t'\) and \(B_t=B_{t^\prime}\cup\{v\}\), then _v_ has no neighbour in \(V(G_{t^\prime})\backslash B_{t^\prime}\). If _t_ is a forget node with child \(t'\) and \(B_t=B_{t^\prime}\backslash\{v\}\), then _v_ has no neighbour outside _V(G<sub>t</sub>_). If _t_ is a join node with children _t_<sub>1</sub>_,t_<sub>2</sub>, then \(V(G_{t_1})\cap V(G_{t_2})=B_t\), and there is no edge between _V(G_<sub>_t_<sub>1</sub></sub>)\\_B<sub>t</sub>_ and _V(G_<sub>_t_<sub>2</sub></sub>)\\_B<sub>t</sub>_.

**Observation 5.** _Let D be an edge open packing of G. Every clique of G contains at most two vertices of V(D), and every edge of G_\[_V(D_)\] _belongs to D._

Both assertions follow from Observation 1: _G_\[_V(D_)\] is a star forest, so it has no triangle, and all its edges are selected.

### 4.1 States

At every node _t_, a state records the vertices of _B<sub>t</sub>_ that are intended to be endpoints of selected edges in the final packing, together with their roles in the partial induced-star forest. We call these vertices _active_. An active vertex is either already incident with a selected edge in the processed part or is pending and must become incident with a selected edge later. Since _B<sub>t</sub>_ is a clique, Observation 5 implies that a state has at most two active vertices.

The possible states are the following.

• The empty state \(\varnothing\) means that no vertex of _B<sub>t</sub>_ is active.<tbc>

• A singleton state \((x,\lambda)\) has \(x\in B_t\) and \(\lambda\in\{P,C,L\}\). Label _P_ means that _x_ is pending and is not yet incident with a selected edge in the processed part. Label _C_ means that _x_ is the centre of a<tbc>

partial star with at least one edge. Label _L_ means that _x_ is a leaf of a star whose centre lies outside the bag and has at least two selected neighbours. In particular, a _K_2 meeting the bag only at _x_ always has label _C_, irrespective of any earlier orientation. • A pair state \((\{x,y\},\lambda)\) has distinct \(x,y\in B_t\) and \(\lambda\in\{E,S_x,S_y\}\). Since _Bt_ is a clique, \(xy\in E(G)\). In every pair state, _xy_ is selected but has not yet been counted. Label _E_ means that _xy_ currently forms a _K_2-component with no counted attachment at either endpoint. Label _Sx_ means that the partial star is centred at _x_ with _y_ as a leaf and at least one counted edge from _x_ to a leaf outside the bag. Label _Sy_ is defined symmetrically. A partial solution at _t_ is a set \(U\subseteq V(G_t)\) such that _H=Gt_\[_U_\] is a disjoint union of stars with at least one edge, with the possible addition of one isolated vertex in _Bt_. The active vertices are exactly \(U\cap B_t\), and every edge of _H_ is selected. The component meeting the bag, if any, has the canonical label defined above; an isolated active vertex has label _P_. There is at most one such component because the bag is a clique. All components disjoint from the bag are complete. For a state \(\sigma\), the table entry \(\mathrm{DP}[t,\sigma]\) is the maximum number of edges of _H_ with at least one endpoint outside _Bt_ over partial solutions with state \(\sigma\), or \(-\infty\) if none exists. Thus, the counting invariant is that every selected edge outside the bag has been counted, while no edge entirely inside the bag has been counted. The latter case occurs only for the edge _xy_ in a pair state; it is counted when the first of _x,y_ is forgotten. Canonical labels depend on the current partial star, so the two endpoints of a _K_2 need not be assigned permanent roles. ## 4.2 Transitions All updates are maximum updates. Entries not produced by a listed transition remain equal to \(-\infty\). **Leaf node.** For a leaf _t_ with empty bag, set \(\mathrm{DP}[t,\varnothing]=0\). **Introduce node.** Let _t_ be an introduce node with child \(t'\) and \(B_t=B_{t^\prime}\cup\{v\}\). The vertex _v_ may be left inactive, so every child state is copied to the same state at _t_ with the same value. If _v_ becomes active, the possible updates are \(\mathrm{DP}[t,(v,P)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(v,P)],\mathrm{DP}[t',\varnothing]\},\)
\(\mathrm{DP}[t,(\{x,v\},E)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(\{x,v\},E)],\mathrm{DP}[t',(x,P)]\},\)
\(\mathrm{DP}[t,(\{x,v\},S_x)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(\{x,v\},S_x)],\mathrm{DP}[t',(x,C)]\},\) for every \(x\in B_{t^\prime}\) for which the child entry is finite. No other transition that makes _v_ active is allowed. Activating _v_ from (_x,L_) would give the leaf _x_ a second selected neighbour, while activating it from a pair state would create three active vertices in a clique. No selected edge is counted at an introduce node. **Forget node.** Let _t_ be a forget node with child \(t'\) and \(B_t=B_{t^\prime}\backslash\{v\}\). If _v_ does not occur in a child state \(\sigma\), copy the state unchanged. The state (_v,P_) is rejected because _v_ would be forgotten before becoming incident with a selected edge. For \(\lambda\in\{C,L\}\), the state \((v,\lambda)\) produces the empty state at _t_ with the same value. Now suppose that the child state is a pair state involving _v_ and another vertex \(x\in B_t\). The selected edge _vx_ is counted at this forget step. The updates are \(\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,C)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,C)],\mathrm{DP}[t',(\{v,x\},E)]+1\},\)
\(\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,L)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,L)],\mathrm{DP}[t',(\{v,x\},S_v)]+1\},\)
\(\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,C)]\leftarrow\mathrm{max}\{\mathrm{DP}[t,(x,C)],\mathrm{DP}[t',(\{v,x\},S_x)]+1\}.\) The first update views the counted _K_2 as a star centred at its remaining endpoint. In the second update, _v_ is the forgotten centre and _x_ remains a leaf; the positive attachment in _Sv_ ensures that _v_ has at least two selected neighbours. In the third, _x_ remains the centre. **Join node.** Let _t_ be a join node with children _t_1_,t_2, where _Bt=B__t_1=_B__t_2. Two child states are combined only when they activate the same subset of _Bt_. Define a partial merge operation ⋆ on labels. For the empty state, \(\varnothing\star\varnothing=\varnothing\). For singleton states on the same vertex, the valid merges are \(P\star P=P,P\star C=C,C\star P=C,\)
\(P\star L=L,L\star P=L,C\star C=C.\)

<tbc>The merges _L⋆L_, _C⋆L_, and _L⋆C_ are invalid. They would create a path with three edges: a label _L_ already places the active vertex at a leaf of a star with at least two edges, and the other nonpending child adds a second neighbour to that leaf.

For pair states on the same two vertices _x,y_, the valid merges are

\(\begin{array}{ c c c }
E\star E=E, & E\star S_x=S_x, & S_x\star E=S_x, \\
E\star S_y=S_y, & S_y\star E=S_y, & S_x\star S_x=S_x, \\
 &  & S_y\star S_y=S_y.
\end{array}\)

The merges _S<sub>x</sub>⋆S<sub>y</sub>_ and _S<sub>y</sub>⋆S<sub>x</sub>_ are invalid because they would place attachments at both endpoints of _xy_.

The join recurrence is

\(\mathrm{DP}[t,\tau]=\mathrm{max}_{\sigma_1\star\sigma_2=\tau}\big\{\mathrm{DP}[t_1,\sigma_1]+\mathrm{DP}[t_2,\sigma_2]\big\},\)

where undefined merges are ignored. No edge is counted at a join node. An edge entirely inside the bag remains uncounted in both children, while every selected edge with an endpoint outside the bag belongs to exactly one child subtree and has already been counted there.

## 4.3 Correctness

The root bag is empty, so the only accepting state at the root _r_ is \(\varnothing\). The value returned by the algorithm is \(\mathrm{DP}[r,\varnothing]\).

**Lemma 6.** _Every finite DP entry satisfies the invariant. Consequently, every accepting computation at the root represents an edge open packing whose cardinality is its DP value._

_Proof._ We argue by induction over the nice tree decomposition. The statement is immediate at a leaf.

At an introduce node, an inactive introduced vertex does not change the partial solution. An active introduced vertex can interact only with active vertices already in the current bag, because it has no neighbour in \(V(G_{t^\prime})\backslash B_{t^\prime}\). The transition from the empty state creates a pending vertex; the transition from (_x,P_) selects _xv_ and creates a _K_<sub>2</sub>-component; and the transition from (_x,C_) attaches _v_ as a new leaf of the star centred at _x_. The excluded cases are precisely those that would give a leaf a second selected neighbour or place three active vertices in one clique. Thus, every introduce transition preserves the invariant.

At a forget node, a pending singleton is rejected. If a singleton centre or leaf is forgotten, its component is complete; the separation property implies that the forgotten vertex has no neighbour outside _V(G<sub>t</sub>_). If _v_ belongs to a pair state with _x_, the edge _vx_ is counted once and the remaining role of _x_ is recorded correctly. Thus, all forget transitions preserve the invariant and count each selected edge exactly once.

At a join node, put _X<sub>i</sub>=V(G<sub>t<sub>i</sub></sub>_)\\_B<sub>t</sub>_ for \(i\in\{1,2\}\). There is no edge between _X_<sub>1</sub> and _X_<sub>2</sub>, so no hidden common edge can be created between selected vertices lying strictly in different child subtrees. All interactions occur through the common bag. Requiring equal active subsets and using the listed merge table preserves exactly the compatible partial-star shapes. In particular, all attachments of a boundary edge lie at the same endpoint. No selected edge is counted twice.

At the root, there is no pending vertex and no uncounted boundary edge. The selected vertices therefore induce a disjoint union of induced stars. By Observation 1, the selected edges form an edge open packing, and every selected edge has been counted exactly once.

**Lemma 7.** _Every edge open packing of G is represented by the dynamic program._

_Proof._ Let _D_ be an edge open packing, and set \(U_t=V(D)\cap V(G_t)\) at each node _t_. Every vertex in _V(G<sub>t</sub>_)\\_B<sub>t</sub>_ has no neighbour outside _V(G<sub>t</sub>_), by the separation property of a tree decomposition. Thus, each vertex of _U<sub>t</sub>_\\_B<sub>t</sub>_ has a selected neighbour in _U<sub>t</sub>_. It follows that _G<sub>t</sub>_\[_U<sub>t</sub>_\] is a star forest whose only possible isolated vertex lies in the bag. Observation 5 ensures that at most two vertices are active, and two active vertices form a selected edge.

Assign each boundary component its canonical label. In particular, a boundary edge _xy_ receives label _E_ exactly when it has no attachment in the processed part; otherwise all attachments have the same centre, giving _S<sub>x</sub>_ or _S<sub>y</sub>_. If a singleton boundary vertex _x_ lies in a partial _K_<sub>2</sub> with its other endpoint _v_ outside the bag, label _C_ is sufficient. Indeed, all selected neighbours of _v_ already lie in _V(G<sub>t</sub>_). If _v_ were the centre of a larger global star, that star would therefore already be present in the processed part. Consequently, this _K_<sub>2</sub> either remains a _K_<sub>2</sub> globally or can grow only at _x_. More generally, the unique centre of a global star with at least two edges cannot be forgotten while one of its leaves remains outside<tbc>

<tbc>the processed graph. When its centre is forgotten and a leaf remains in the bag, the partial component already has at least two edges and receives label _L_.

At an introduce node, a newly active vertex is pending, is joined to a pending vertex to form a _K_<sub>2</sub>, or is attached to a known centre. These are exactly the listed transitions. At a forget node, a pending vertex cannot occur in the restriction of _D_, because it has no selected neighbour in the processed graph and no neighbour outside it. The other forget transitions preserve the canonical label and count the edge between two active vertices, if present.

At a join node, the two child partial solutions are restrictions of the same global packing and therefore activate the same bag vertices. For a singleton, a leaf with label _L_ in one child has no selected neighbour in the other child and hence meets label _P_ there. Otherwise the labels belong to {_P,C_}, whose merges are all listed. For a boundary edge _xy_, all counted attachments lie at the same endpoint, so its pair labels also combine by a valid merge. Induction now gives a DP computation representing _D_ and counting each of its edges exactly once.

Lemmas 6 and 7 imply that \(\mathrm{DP}[r,\varnothing]=\rho_\mathrm{e}^\circ(G)\).

### 4.4 Running time and reconstruction

Let _b<sub>t</sub>_=|_B<sub>t</sub>_|. A table contains one empty state, 3_b<sub>t</sub>_ singleton states, and \(3\genfrac(){pt}{2}{b_t}{2}\) pair states, hence _O_((_b<sub>t</sub>_+1)<sup>2</sup>) states. Leaf, introduce, and forget nodes can be processed in _O_((_b<sub>t</sub>_+1)<sup>2</sup>) time.

At a join node, states are grouped by their active subset. There is one label for the empty subset, three labels for each singleton subset, and three labels for each two-element subset. Thus, only constantly many label pairs are examined for each active subset, and a join node also takes _O_((_b<sub>t</sub>_+1)<sup>2</sup>) time. The nice decomposition has _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) nodes and \(b_t\le n\), so the total running time is _O(n_<sup>4</sup>).

For a disconnected graph with component orders _n_<sub>1</sub>_,...,n<sub>q</sub>_, the total running time is \(O(\sum_in_i^4)\subseteq O(n^4)\). To reconstruct an optimum packing, store a predecessor transition for every improving DP update and backtrack from the root. This does not change the asymptotic time bound.

**Theorem 8.** _For a chordal graph G on n vertices, the dynamic program computes_ \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\circ(G)\) _and an optimum edge open packing in O(n_<sup>4</sup>) _time._

## 5 Maximum Edge Open Packing in Convex Bipartite Graphs

Let \(G=(X\cup Y,E)\) be a convex bipartite graph. Isolated vertices do not affect an edge open packing and are deleted first; if no edge remains, the optimum is zero. Let _X_={_x_<sub>1</sub>_,x_<sub>2</sub>_,...,x<sub>p</sub>_} be a convex ordering. For each \(y\in Y\) , write \(N(y)=\{x_{\ell(y)},x_{\ell(y)+1},\dots,x_{r(y)}\}\).

By Observation 1, the components of _G_\[_V(D_)\] for an edge open packing _D_ are stars _K_<sub>1_,t_</sub> with \(t\ge 1\). In particular, _K_<sub>2</sub> is included. Its centre may be chosen in either part; when describing an existing packing, we choose its endpoint in _X_. Since _X_ and _Y_ are independent sets, a collection of vertex-disjoint stars forms an edge open packing exactly when there is no edge between two distinct stars.

### 5.1 Separation properties

For a component _S_ of _G_\[_V(D_)\], define \(x_\mathrm{min}(S)=\mathrm{min}\{i:x_i\in V(S)\cap X\}\). Every component contains an edge, so this minimum is defined. List the components as _S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>_ in increasing order of _x_<sub>min</sub>; their minima are distinct because their vertex sets are disjoint. A _prefix_ is S_<sub>j</sub>_={_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>j</sub>_} for some \(0\le j\le k\), with \(\mathcal{S}_0=\varnothing\). A component _S<sub>t</sub>_ is _later_ than this prefix if _t\>j_.

**Claim 9.** _If a\<b, every X-vertex of S<sub>a</sub> has index smaller than x_<sub>min</sub>(_S<sub>b</sub>)._

_Proof._ Put _i=x_<sub>min</sub>(_S<sub>b</sub>_). An _X_-centred star contains just one _X_-vertex. Otherwise, if _S<sub>a</sub>_ contained _X_- vertices on both sides of index _i_, convexity would make its _Y_ -centre adjacent to _x<sub>i</sub>_, joining two distinct components. Equality of indices is excluded by vertex-disjointness.

For a prefix S, define \(\alpha(\mathcal{S})=\mathrm{max}\{i:x_i\in V(S)\cap X\text{for some}S\in\mathcal{S}\}\) and \(\beta(\mathcal{S})=\mathrm{max}\{r(y):y\in V(S)\cap Y\text{for some}S\in\mathcal{S}\}\), taking both maxima to be zero for the empty prefix. We always have \(\alpha(\mathcal{S})\le\beta(\mathcal{S})\): each selected _X_-vertex has a selected _Y_ -neighbour whose right endpoint is at least its index.

**Lemma 10.** _Let_ S _be a prefix, and put_ \(\alpha=\alpha(\mathcal{S})\) _and_ \(\beta=\beta(\mathcal{S})\)_. In every later component, each X-vertex x<sub>i</sub> satisfies_ \(i>\beta\)_, and each Y-vertex y satisfies_ \(\ell(y)>\alpha\).

_Proof._ The empty-prefix case is immediate. Suppose that a later selected vertex _x<sub>i</sub>_ satisfies \(i\le\beta\). A previously selected _Y_ -vertex _y_ has \(r(y)=\beta\) and a selected neighbour _x<sub>h</sub>_ in its component. Claim 9 gives _h\<i_, so \(\ell(y)\le h<i\le r(y)\). Convexity implies \(yx_i\in E(G)\), a contradiction. Thus \(i>\beta\ge\alpha\).

If a later selected _Y_ -vertex _z_ had \(\ell(z)\le\alpha\), its selected neighbour _x<sub>i</sub>_ would satisfy \(\ell(z)\le\alpha<i\le r(z)\). It would therefore be adjacent to the previously selected vertex \(x_\alpha\), again a contradiction.

## 5.2 Dynamic programming table

A _labelled partial solution_ consists of an edge open packing \(D'\) together with barriers \((\alpha,\beta)\). Its components are generated from left to right by the transitions below. The value \(\alpha\) is the exact index of its rightmost selected _X_-vertex, with \(\alpha=0\) only for the empty solution. The recorded barrier \(\beta\) is an upper bound on _r(y_) for every selected \(y\in Y\) . It may exceed their actual maximum; such a conservative barrier restricts the permitted continuation. In every reachable state \(\alpha\le\beta\). The continuation rule requires every future selected _X_-vertex to have index greater than \(\beta\) and every future selected _Y_ -vertex _y_ to satisfy \(\ell(y)>\alpha\).

For \(0\le\alpha,\beta\le p\), let \(F[\alpha,\beta]\) be the maximum number of edges in a reachable labelled partial solution with these barriers, or \(-\infty\) if none exists. Future choices depend only on the barriers, so retaining the largest value for each pair is sufficient. Initialize _F_\[0,0\]=0 and all other entries to \(-\infty\). Each transition strictly increases \(\beta\): its new value is either \(q\ge i>\beta\) or \(r(y)\ge q\ge s>\beta\). The states can therefore be processed in increasing order of \(\beta\).

## 5.3 Transitions

We append one new star component to a reachable partial solution.

**_X_-centred star.** Choose a centre _x<sub>i</sub>_ with \(i>\beta\) and a new right-endpoint barrier \(q\in\{i,\dots,p\}\). Define<tbc>

\(w_X(i,\alpha,q)=\big|\{y\in Y:\alpha<\ell(y)\le i\le r(y)\le q\}\big|.\)

<tbc>If \(w_X(i,\alpha,q)>0\), select all these vertices as leaves and update

\(F[i,q]\leftarrow max\{F[i,q],F[\alpha,\beta]+w_X(i,\alpha,q)\}.\)

The condition \(i>\beta\) excludes edges from the new centre to previously selected _Y_ -vertices, and \(\ell(y)>\alpha\) excludes edges from new leaves to previously selected _X_-vertices. The updated barriers require future _X_-vertices to lie beyond _q_ and future _Y_ -vertices to have left endpoint greater than _i_; hence the new star is also separated from all permitted future components. The recorded value _q_ need not be attained by a selected leaf, which is why conservative barriers are allowed.

**_Y_ -centred star.** Choose a centre \(y\in Y\) with \(\ell(y)>\alpha\), and put \(s=max\{\ell(y),\beta+1\}\). If \(s\le r(y)\), then for every \(q\in\{s,\dots,r(y)\}\) select _x<sub>s</sub>,...,x<sub>q</sub>_ as leaves and update

\(F[q,r(y)]\leftarrow max\{F[q,r(y)],F[\alpha,\beta]+q-s+1\}.\)

The new leaves have indices greater than \(\beta\), so they are nonadjacent to previously selected _Y_ -vertices. The condition \(\ell(y)>\alpha\) separates the new centre from previously selected _X_-vertices. Future _Y_ -vertices have left endpoint greater than _q_, and future _X_-vertices have index greater than _r(y_), so neither can have an edge to the new star.

The algorithm returns \(max_{0\le\alpha,\beta\le p}F[\alpha,\beta]\).

## 5.4 Correctness

**Lemma 11.** _Every solution constructed by the dynamic program is an edge open packing._

_Proof._ Both transitions add a star whose vertices have no edges to earlier selected vertices, as shown above, and preserve the stated barrier invariants. In particular, no previously selected vertex can be reused: a previous _X_-vertex has index at most \(\alpha\le\beta\), while a previous _Y_ -vertex has a selected neighbour of index at most \(\alpha\) and therefore has left endpoint at most \(\alpha\). Inductively, the selected vertices induce disjoint stars, and Observation 1 applies.

**Lemma 12.** _For every edge open packing D, the dynamic program constructs a solution of cardinality at least_ |_D|._

_Proof._ Process _S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>_ in their defined order, possibly adding leaves. We maintain the exact barriers of the corresponding original prefix and keep the enlarged prefix compatible with the unprocessed components. Initially both barriers are zero. Suppose the current barriers are \(\alpha,\beta\), and _S_ is the next component. Lemma 10 gives index greater than \(\beta\) for every _X_-vertex of _S_, and left endpoint greater than \(\alpha\) for every _Y_ -vertex of _S_.

If _S_ is centred at \(x_i\in X\), let \(q=max\{r(y):y\in V(S)\cap Y\}\). Every original leaf is counted by \(w_X(i,\alpha,q)\), so the corresponding transition selects at least |_E(S_)| edges. An added leaf has left endpoint greater than \(\alpha\) and right endpoint at most _q_, excluding edges to all earlier selected _X_-vertices. Applying Lemma 10 to the original prefix including _S_ shows that every later selected _X_-vertex has index greater than _q_, excluding edges to these vertices as well. An added leaf cannot already belong to a later component, since its edge to _x<sub>i</sub>_ would join that component to _S_. Since an original leaf attains _q_ and \(q\ge i>\beta\), the enlarged prefix has exact barriers (_i,q_), the same as the original prefix including _S_.

If _S_ is centred at \(y\in Y\) , put \(q=max\{h:x_h\in V(S)\cap X\}\) and \(s=max\{\ell(y),\beta+1\}\). All original leaves lie in _x<sub>s</sub>,...,x<sub>q</sub>_, so the transition again selects at least |_E(S_)| edges. Any added leaf has index greater than \(\beta\), excluding edges to previously selected _Y_ -vertices. Applying Lemma 10 to the original prefix including _S_ shows that every later selected _Y_ -vertex _z_ satisfies \(\ell(z)>q\). Thus none of the added leaves has an edge to a later selected _Y_ -vertex. Claim 9 also ensures that none is a selected _X_-vertex of a later component. The exact barriers are (_q,r(y_)), unchanged from those of the original prefix including _S_, since _x<sub>q</sub>_ is an original leaf and \(r(y)\ge q>\beta\).

Both transitions therefore preserve the induction invariant. Their sequence gives a reachable value at least |_D_|.

### 5.5 Running time and reconstruction

Deleting isolated vertices and extracting interval endpoints from a given convex ordering takes _O(n+m_) time. If an ordering is not supplied, it can be found in _O(n+m_) time by consecutive-ones testing \[2\].

The table has (_p_+1)<sup>2</sup>=_O(p_<sup>2</sup>) entries. Compute \(C[a,b]=|\{y\in Y:\ell(y)=a,r(y)=b\}|\) for \(1\le a\le b\le p\), with zero entries elsewhere. A two-dimensional prefix-sum table gives \(w_X(i,\alpha,q)=\sum_{a=\alpha+1}^i\sum_{b=i}^QC[a,b]\) in _O_(1) time. This preprocessing takes _O(p_<sup>2</sup>+|_Y_|) time and space. From one state there are _O(p_<sup>2</sup>) _X_-centred transitions and _O_(|_Y|p_) _Y_ -centred transitions. The total time is therefore _O(p_<sup>4</sup>+_p_<sup>3</sup>|_Y_|)=_O(n_<sup>4</sup>).

For each improving update, store its predecessor state, transition type, centre, and endpoint _q_. Backtracking identifies at most _p_ transitions, since \(\beta\) strictly increases. Recover the leaves of each _X_-centred star by scanning _Y_ , and those of each _Y_ -centred star by listing its selected interval. Reconstruction takes _O(p|Y_|+_p_<sup>2</sup>) time. The tables, interval endpoints, and predecessor records use _O(p_<sup>2</sup>+|_Y_|) auxiliary space once the ordering is available; including the input and ordering preprocessing, _O(n_<sup>2</sup>) space suffices.

**Theorem 13.** _The_ Maximum Edge Open Packing _problem can be solved in O(n_<sup>4</sup>) _time and O(n_<sup>2</sup>) _space on convex bipartite graphs._

_Proof._ Lemma 11 bounds the returned value from above by \(\rho_\mathrm{e}^\mathrm{o}(G)\), and Lemma 12 gives the reverse inequality. The preceding analysis establishes the time and space bounds and the reconstruction of an optimum packing.

## 6 Conclusion

We proved that the oriented star-conflict graph of Das and Santra \[13\] preserves AT-freeness and used this property to obtain an _O(n_<sup>2</sup>+_m_<sup>4</sup>)-time algorithm for Maximum Edge Open Packing on AT-free graphs. We also gave _O(n_<sup>4</sup>)-time dynamic programs for chordal and convex bipartite graphs. The former handles unbounded clique number, while the latter extends the earlier biconvex algorithm.

Natural next questions are whether these running times can be improved and whether Maximum Edge Open Packing admits a polynomial-time algorithm on chordal bipartite graphs. Distance- hereditary graphs are already covered by Bhyravarapu et al. \[1\]. It is also useful to study further classes for which the construction \(G\mapsto A_G\) preserves a structure that makes maximum independent set tractable.

For general graphs, fixed-parameter tractability by treewidth follows from monadic second-order optimisation \[10\]: feasibility of a chosen edge set is expressed by excluding two selected edges together with a third edge joining their endpoints, and the objective is its cardinality. Thus, the questions concern explicit algorithms, their dependence on treewidth, and kernelisation bounds. An independent set _S_ is asteroidal if _S_\\{_v_} lies in one component of _G-N<sub>G</sub>_\[_v_\] for every \(v\in S\); its maximum size is the asteroidal<tbc>

number. The preservation proof maps an asteroidal set of _A<sub>G</sub>_ to an asteroidal set of _G_ by taking the leaf coordinates: the same path argument applies to any two members while avoiding a third. Combined with the bounded-asteroidal-number result of Broersma et al. [6], this gives polynomial-time solvability for each fixed bound on asteroidal number. Whether the dependence can be made fixed-parameter tractable is a more precise further question.
